outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Case Context and Procedural History
outline.description: This chapter establishes the factual backdrop of the Jimenez family's flight from Colombia and traces the procedural journey through the immigration system. It details the specific events constituting the alleged persecution, including political campaigning, the property dispute with a narco-trafficker, and subsequent threats. Crucially, it outlines the procedural posture, explaining how the case moved from the Immigration Judge (IJ) to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) and finally to the Tenth Circuit, setting the stage for appellate review.
subtopics: Petitioners' Profile: Family origins, political affiliation (Colombian Liberal Party), and professional roles (lawyer/intern)
Timeline of Alleged Harms: From political threats in 2022 to direct confrontations with 'Don Rafa'
The Property Dispute Incident: How Jimenez's investigation into narco-trafficking properties triggered escalation
Procedural Posture: The sequence of Notice to Appear, IJ denial, BIA affirmation, and appeal to the Tenth Circuit
Scope of Appeal: Clarifying that Petitioners only challenge asylum/withholding claims, not CAT or due process

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Standards of Review and Legal Framework for Asylum
outline.description: This chapter defines the legal lens through which the court analyzes the case. It explains the statutory definition of a 'refugee' under the INA and breaks down the three-prong test required for asylum eligibility based on past persecution. Furthermore, it articulates the deferential 'substantial evidence' standard applied by appellate courts when reviewing factual findings made by immigration judges and the BIA.
subtopics: Statutory Definition of Refugee: The requirement of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion
Past Persecution vs. Well-Founded Fear: The relationship between establishing past harm and presuming future danger
The Three Elements of Past Persecution: Severity/harm level, protected ground nexus, and government involvement/control
Standard of Review: Understanding why 'substantial evidence' makes overturning BIA/IJ findings difficult
Burden of Proof: The petitioner's obligation to prove eligibility by a preponderance of the evidence

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Analyzing Past Persecution – Severity and Cumulative Harm
outline.description: Focusing on Section II.C of the opinion, this chapter dissects why threats alone failed to constitute persecution. It explores how courts distinguish between 'offensive' harm that rises to persecution versus mere harassment or sporadic threats. The analysis highlights how the court aggregated various incidents (phone calls, brochures, gunpoint encounters) yet still found them insufficient due to a lack of physical injury or lasting psychological trauma severe enough to meet legal thresholds.
subtopics: 'Threats Alone Are Insufficient': Precedent distinguishing verbal threats from actionable persecution
outline: How courts evaluate multiple incidents together versus in isolation
outline.Physical vs. Psychological Harm: Why emo: Comparison with precedents rejecting similar fact patterns (e.g., Chhetri v. Rosen)
outline.How admitting a lack of physical harm we: Why speculative future harm does not cure past insufficiency
